newsitem.title: INDIA: FEATURE-Pakistan, partition loomed with Indian free.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Pakistan, partition loomed with Indian free.

text.p: NEW DELHI, Aug 8 - A golden map of India with a couple of Moslem green splashes and the words "Our Demand" sat above the fireplace in Mohammad Ali Jinnah's study in a white house on the road named after Emperor Aurangzeb, last of the great Moghuls.

Within days, the words would read: "Our Realisation". The splashes marked East and West Pakistan, chunks of land on either side of independent India which Jinnah, the founder of the new state of Pakistan, had fought hard for.
THE PASSING OF AN EMPIRE

The viceroy, members of the interim government and battalions of secretaries and partition officials had in front of them a less ornamental design -- a calendar showing the number of days left before August 15, 1947, before the passing of an empire.

Boundary Commissions were only just getting down to work, but the physical shape of the bisected Islamic state -- lopping the left shoulder off India and revising geography -- already existed in the minds of millions.
Although trainloads of personnel and tons of files had to be shifted in one of the greatest and most hurried flittings over, Karachi had already been identified as the capital of Pakistan.
Islamabad was later to become the capital.
Jinnah was born in a modest house there on Christmas Day in 1876.

Masses of statistics were produced on the economies of India and Pakistan. Pakistan had plenty of food -- a net grain surplus of 500,000 tons -- and Western Pakistan could amply afford to make good the deficiency in Eastern Pakistan.
India, however, would be short of food. Even with a daily twelve-ounce ration, belt tightening would be necessary.

Though the partition of the Punjab and Bengal would exclude mineral and power resources and weaken Pakistan's economy, Moslem economists maintained the new state, with bargaining capital in its fertile fields, would be quite able to stand on its own feet.
Pakistan was industrially backward compared to India, lacking coal, iron ore, rubber, cloth, sugar, paper and matches.

But the partition of the Punjab and Bengal was not a total loss to Pakistan. In the case of Punjab it would mean the severance of the famine-stricken areas of Ambala, which had long been a liability to the province.

Eastern Pakistan, which became Bangladesh in 1971, supplied about 85 per cent of the world's raw jute. Pakistan also had more than a quarter of British India's sheep and goats, one-third of its cattle and about half of its horses, mules, donkeys and camels.
The economies of India and Pakistan were expected to be complementary for some time. Both countries would be losers unless close economic co-operation existed.
PARTITION OBSESSION

There was a sort of partition obsession in Delhi at the time. It covered everything, from the most efficient army in the East to typewriter ribbons. There were special committees galore covering every aspect of the split.
Since July 1946 thousands of Moslems working in Delhi's imperial red sandstone Secretariat had been moved to the west. Sixteen specially chartered trains ferried them 900 miles to Karachi.
A story circulated that 20 years before in Bombay's plush Taj hotel, an Irish woman claiming the power to tell fortunes told Mr Jinnah -- "You will be ruler of your own state one day."
One newspaper commented: "Who is this Irish Lady? If she is found she may well claim to be appointed astrologer-general of the Quaid-e-Azam's government."
Quaid-e-Azam means Supreme Leader. Jinnah's critics said he would be a virtual dictator of his Islamic State and that it might more appropriately be called Jinnahstan than Pakistan.

Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru and other Congress leaders never talked about "Hindustan". India, less two provinces, half-provinces, a residency and a district, remained India and they were sure that in the fullness of time, India would be one again.
It remained to be seen whether the future of the sub-continent brought to millions of Indians any more freedom from the want, hunger and disease that had cursed them for so many years.
